It sets itself apart from standard delta tracking by producing samples proportional to $T(t)$ directly, whereas standard delta tracking produces samples proportional to $\sigma_t(t)T(t)$ (the probability of the *first* interaction) [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that standard delta tracking samples a free-flight distance $t_1$ with probability density $p_1(t) = sigma_t(t) T(t)$. It then describes a technique (differential delta tracking) that transforms these samples to produce a weighted sample density $p_2(t) = T(0, t)$, which is proportional to the transmittance $T(t)$. Thus, the claim that the new method produces samples proportional to $T(t)$ while standard delta tracking produces samples proportional to $sigma_t(t)T(t)$ is fully supported by the text.

Specifically, the expected value of the weight $w$ over many samples equals $C$ [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that the sampling weight $w$ (defined as $t_1$ or $t_2/s$) serves to 'provide an unbiased estimate of the normalization constant $C$'. In statistical estimation, if a weighted sample provides an unbiased estimate of a constant $C$, it implies that the expected value of the weight $w$ over many samples equals $C$. Specifically, the text notes that $w$ 'captures the difference between our unnormalized target density $T$ and the normalized density' and is 'exactly the area under the curve of the binary function', which integrates to $C$.
